# C A U T E R Y.

<margin>15.</margin>
Therefore, pus is blood corrupted in the very part where the wound is, and it is the result of a digestion <note>digestion: in Helmontian terms, the transformative process of vital energy upon matter</note> that has been impaired in that same place. Thus, to have impaired the integrity, continuity, and digestion of the parts, and finally to have converted blood into pus, is what has been held in the *Schools* to mean that one has countered a *Catarrh* <gloss>a "down-flow" of waste fluids from the head</gloss>: whether by having extracted through the hole of the cautery an excrementitious humor (which otherwise had threatened to descend to a <term>noble part</term> <gloss>a vital internal organ like the heart or liver</gloss>) from the head (where they all originally seek the source of *Catarrhs*): or whether in the meantime there is a consensus with the wounded part in the head, or not; for it is all the same, provided the wounded skin is kept occupied. Whether that excrementitious humor be blood, or whether it becomes pus, or <term>sanies</term> <gloss>a thin, greenish or bloody discharge</gloss>, it is all the same, provided that the world is deceived by the worn-out terms of Catarrh, precaution, derivation, revulsion, and the fontanelle <gloss>an artificial drain or issue</gloss>. For I observe a yearling infant, now teething, both suffering from a fever, foam at the mouth, and incessant saliva. And finally, there are cramps, and stools of a yellowish-green. At least that tooth is a part of the head; wherefore the diarrhea will be a catarrh of the head. But what is the consensus of the erupting tooth, or of the swollen gum, with the intestine? Or what is its power of generating, of admitting a Catarrh from the infant's stomach to the head? And thence into the *Ileon* <gloss>the lower part of the small intestine</gloss>? By what right will a vapor distilled from the stomach become greenish bile in the head? Has the workshop of bile perhaps migrated to the head since the beginning of life? Could a cautery (if the infant were capable of enduring it) drive the porraceous <gloss>leek-green</gloss> diarrhea into itself? And compensate for several pounds of porraceous bile with a few tiny drops of pus? Why does the infant's stomach manufacture a Catarrh on account of a toothache? Why is it sent into the Intestine, and not to the aching tooth? Does the reader not yet see that diarrhea is not a Catarrh? But rather that the indignant *Archeus* <gloss>the vital, internal energy that governs organ function</gloss>, wherever it may be, is ready in the Intestine to transmute the alimentary chyme into excrements, which are thought by the *Schools* to be bile, phlegm, etc. If, therefore, diarrhea is not a Catarrh, and the indignant *Archeus* can transmute 

<column-break/>

any matter into a hostile liquid, provided only that the gum is afflicted, can it not then discharge itself in every direction through the established emunctories <gloss>cleansing channels or pores</gloss>? And must it wait for a skin opened by a caustic? Ah, cruel dullness, has it made the *Schools* rage against mortals who are related to them?
<margin>16.</margin>
For they do not even consider that in women, and in obese people, there is a fleshy membrane around the ordinary places for a cautery, mere lard to a thickness of at least two fingers, yet it is to these persons that more frequent, and supposedly more beneficial, cauteries are recommended. Wherefore the bottom of the fontanelle will barely reach the middle of the lard.
<margin>17.</margin>
There is, therefore, no path by which a bad humor, a fictitious *Catarrh* proscribed by its own fault, may rush from the brain, or between the skull and the skin, through the middle of the fat. But what, finally, is that solitary humor, which, proscribed by the part that sends it forth on account of its own sin, descends unmixed through the substance of the fat, and degenerates into pus? If it is an exhalation of vapors from the stomach, why will it not be more frequent in the young and those with hot stomachs, than in the weak, the old, and the cold? By what method will this water, distilled from a vapor, put on the form of pus? How will it hasten through the brain, the meninges, and the skull to find the hole made by the cautery, so that it may flow out and be purged only by that path? Why does the vapor not fly off into the air a hundred times before it reaches the place designed by the willing cautery? How will water rising from the stomach become blood and the matter of pus? How will blood (the matter of pus, according to *Galen*) be the matter of *Catarrh*? Why must blood be reduced into the series of bad humors, which, not yet contaminated, is dispensed by nature to the wounded place? Why, once the wound is made, will nature cease to disturb the condemned matter through and into the places accustomed to it? For, once the skin is opened at the whim of the healer, will it become ignorant of its deviations? Or has it perhaps labored only so that it might find an exit somewhere? And that having been done, will it henceforth come into the service of the one wounding it? Therefore, these four things are false,

<summary>Van Helmont critiques the medical theory of cauterization, arguing that the discharge from an artificial wound is not a "catarrh" being purged from the body, but rather healthy blood being corrupted by the local trauma. He challenges the logical consistency of physicians who claim such fluids travel through layers of fat and bone, dismissing these explanations as scholastic inventions that ignore physiological reality.</summary>
<keywords>cautery, fontanelle, Archeus, pus, medical theory, Schools, catarrh, Galen, humors, physiology</keywords>
